One-sentence thesis: GC finds heap objects that are no longer reachable from roots and reclaims them. Your job is to manage pauses and leaks — not to recite flags.
Answer every GC question with: Mechanism → Trade-off → Measurement → Decision

1 · JVM memory map

STACK HEAP METASPACE
RegionWhat lives hereGC?
StackPer-thread call frames, locals, referencesNo — auto cleared
HeapEverything created with newYes — GC’s only job site
MetaspaceClass metadata (native memory)Outside the Java heap; unlimited by default
Story — the office building: Stack is each employee’s (thread’s) desk — work ends, desk clears, no janitor. Heap is the shared warehouse — everyone drops boxes with new; the janitor (GC) sweeps only here. Metaspace is the archive room for class blueprints — it can grow even when the heap looks fine.
ProblemPod is OOMKilled, but there is no Java OutOfMemoryError.
SolutionHeap ≠ all JVM memory. Metaspace + thread stacks + direct buffers also consume RAM. Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 and Native Memory Tracking (NMT).
Notebook →GC cleans only the Heap. Stack clears itself. OOMKilled ≠ Java OOM.

2 · What happens on new User()

User u = new User("Ali");

1. Stack

A reference named u (an address) is born.

2. Heap

The User object (with fields) is born.

3. Link

u points to the object. If the link breaks and no other root holds it → garbage candidate.
STACK frame HEAP ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ │ int x = 5 │ │ User │ │ User u ──────┼──────────►│ name = "Ali" │ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────┘
Primitives vs references: int x = 5 stores the value in the stack frame. User u stores only a pointer on the stack; the real object is on the heap. Arrays, Strings, boxed Integers — all objects → heap.
Notebook →Stack holds the reference; Heap holds the object.

3 · What is garbage? Reachability & leaks

Story — GC is an electrician, not a detective: It follows wires from roots (stack locals, static fields, JNI). Lights that turn on are live. Two lamps wired to each other but not to the wall outlet → dark → garbage.
Java memory leak: The object’s job is done — it should be garbage — but something still holds a reference. Classic culprits: static Map / unbounded cache, forgotten ThreadLocal, unregistered listener/callback.
ProblemHeap baseline keeps rising (the bottom of the sawtooth drifts up).
SolutionTake a heap dump → MAT dominator tree → find the retainer → usually static / ThreadLocal / listener.
Notebook →Garbage = unreachable. Leak = should be unreachable, but still on a root chain.

4 · Generational hypothesis

Eden

Newborn objects. Minor GC scans here. Most become gray = garbage.

Survivor S0⇄S1

Survivors are copied; age +1 each GC. Ping-pong between spaces.

Old

Objects past the age threshold (~15). Rare, expensive collections.
TermMeaning
Minor / Young GCCleans Eden (+ Survivors) — frequent, usually short
Major / Old / MixedAlso touches Old — more expensive
STWStop-The-World: app threads pause = PAUSE
STW = Stop-The-World: During some GC phases the whole application freezes. All GC engineering is about shortening and stabilizing that pause.
Notebook →Young = frequent & cheap. Old = rare & expensive. Pause = making users wait.

5 · An object’s life journey

Story — a request DTO: HTTP request arrives → new RequestDto() in Eden → handler finishes → no references → next Minor GC deletes it. That is a good life.

Bad life: you stash the same DTO in static List<RequestDto> ALL → it ages through Survivors → promotes to Old → Mixed/Full GC pain.
ProblemOld fills quickly; short-lived objects promote too early.
Solution1) Reduce allocation 2) Grow heap (more room for Young) 3) Do not set -Xmn with G1.
Notebook →Good objects die in Eden. Accidental retainers force promotion and Old pressure.

6 · Three collectors, three personalities

Parallel

Throughput king. Batch/ETL. Long pauses are OK.

G1

Balanced. Default since Java 9. Start here for most services.

ZGC

Pause ≈ <1ms. Concurrent mark/relocate. Costs CPU + memory. Java 21+.
Golden interview sentence: “I first reduce allocation in code, then measure, and only then change the collector or flags.”
Trap: If the JVM sees <2 CPUs or <~1.8GB memory, it may silently pick Serial GC (common in tiny Kubernetes pods).
Notebook →Service → G1. Batch → Parallel. Proven p99 GC pain → ZGC. Measure before switching.

7 · G1 — the interview star

Regions

  • Heap is split into equal regions (1–32 MB).
  • Roles are not fixed: Eden today, Empty tomorrow, Old later.
  • Humongous: object larger than 50% of a region → special H regions (giant arrays are common culprits).
  • MaxGCPauseMillis = TARGET (not a guarantee), default 200ms.

The G1 cycle

  1. Young GC (STW): evacuate Eden + Survivors into free regions.
  2. Concurrent Mark: starts around IHOP ~45%; application keeps running.
  3. Mixed GC: Young + selected dirty Old regions.
  4. Full GC: last resort, long STW = ALARM.
ProblemHumongous objects
SolutionGrow region size / split the giant array
Problemto-space exhausted
SolutionGrow heap / raise G1ReservePercent
ProblemMark starts too late → Full GC
SolutionLower IHOP / reduce allocation

One-line answers (memorize)

QuestionOne-line answer
Remembered Set / Card Table?Avoid scanning all of Old during Young GC; write barriers keep them updated.
SATB?Snapshot-At-The-Beginning — a “photo” of the heap at mark start for concurrent correctness.
Why not -Xmn with G1?Locks Young size; G1 cannot auto-tune toward the pause goal.
32 GB boundary?Crossing it loses compressed oops (4-byte refs); 33GB can be worse than 30GB.
G1 vs ZGC?Switch only if measurement shows GC pauses break the SLO; ZGC costs CPU/memory.
Notebook →G1 = region-based, pause-targeted, Young + Mixed. Full GC in G1 is an alarm.

8 · Problem → Solution cards

SymptomFirst reflex
Heap baseline risingDump + MAT → leak
Frequent Full GC (G1)Log cause: humongous / to-space / late mark
OOMKilled, no Java OOMMaxRAMPercentage + NMT
p99 spikes, clean GC logSafepoint / swap / CPU throttle
GC overhead limit exceededLeak first; else grow heap
Dump freezes the podDrain from LB; or class_histogram ×2 / JFR
Tight SLO, G1 not enoughMeasure → then ZGC (costs CPU + RAM)
Problemp99 spikes but GC log looks clean
SolutionCheck safepoint logs, swap, k8s CPU throttling — it may not be GC.
ProblemGC overhead limit exceeded
SolutionJVM spends almost all time in GC and reclaims almost nothing → dump for leak, else grow heap.
Notebook →Don’t memorize flags — memorize the diagnosis algorithm: symptom → evidence → action.

9 · Flags, logs & the answer formula

Every GC answer:
1) Mechanism → 2) Trade-off → 3) Measurement (log / JFR / MAT) → 4) Decision (if data shows X…) 
java \
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log \
  -jar app.jar
[2.345s][info][gc] GC(12) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 512M->128M(1024M) 8.1ms
# Pause Young = STW Young GC
# 512M->128M  = used before → after
# (1024M)     = heap capacity
# 8.1ms       = pause duration

Level 1 — memorize

MaxRAMPercentage, UseG1GC/UseZGC, MaxGCPauseMillis, HeapDumpOnOOM, gc logging

Level 2 — if asked

IHOP, G1HeapRegionSize, NMT, JFR, ParallelGC, MaxMetaspaceSize

Level 3 — don’t touch blindly

AlwaysPreTouch, G1ReservePercent, MaxDirectMemorySize, Xss
Do-not-touch list: -Xmn with G1; blind System.gc(); a random 20-flag paste from the internet; tuning without a baseline.
Notebook →Mids recite flags. Seniors measure first, then decide.

10 · GetYourGuide-style mock answers

Read these out loud. Then close the page and reproduce them without looking.

Q: How does GC work?
“Objects live on the heap. GC walks from roots (stack, statics, JNI) and keeps the reachable set; unreachable objects are garbage. Generational collectors gather short-lived objects cheaply in Eden and promote long-lived ones to Old. Pauses (STW) affect user latency, so collector choice is a throughput-vs-latency trade-off. In production I look at allocation and leaks first, then measure, then tune.”
Q: Which GC would you pick?
“For a normal request/response service I start with G1 — pause-targeted and the default. For batch/throughput jobs I’d consider Parallel. If p99 SLO is broken by GC pauses and logs/JFR prove it, I’d try ZGC on Java 21+. I also watch for Serial GC on tiny pods.”
Q: You’re seeing frequent Full GCs — what do you do?
“In G1, Full GC is an alarm. I read the log cause: humongous → grow region / split the object; to-space exhausted → grow heap / reserve; late marking → lower IHOP / cut allocation. In parallel I check for a leak with a heap dump.”
Q: How do you optimize GC?
“1) Mechanism: G1 is region-based with Young + Mixed collections. 2) Trade-off: shorter pauses usually cost more CPU; ZGC also wants more memory. 3) Measurement: GC logs, JFR allocation, MAT if needed. 4) Decision: humongous → region; Old filling → IHOP/allocation; SLO → ZGC. Always cut unnecessary allocation in code first.”
Wall poster: Mids recite flags. Seniors measure first, then decide.
